sm: Kyle Peterson hosts Potomac Watch with Wall Street Journal colleagues Joe Sternberg and Kim Strassel. They discuss a memo from Wisconsin Senator Ron Johnson, outgoing Senate budget chairman, on Social Security's looming insolvency. Johnson notes that life expectancy has risen 17 years while the retirement age rose only two, and that workers per beneficiary fell from 16.5 to 1 in 1950 to 2.6 to 1 in 2025. He calls the program a Ponzi scheme. The panelists say the finances have long been known, with insolvency projected around 2032 and a cut of roughly 22 percent. They say the Ponzi language is imprecise but gets attention, and that the program was designed around a shorter life expectancy and higher birth rates. Strassel recalls George W. Bush's failed push for market accounts and argues reform must be big and bold.

The discussion returns to Johnson's effort to shape the Social Security debate. Sternberg recalls midterm campaigns where Democrats said they would protect benefits, and he questions Johnson's idea of avoiding the 2032 cliff by funding the shortfall from the general budget. Strassel says many people wrongly believe the benefits are their own money, calls it an entitlement program, and says that misunderstanding must be dislodged. She explains that Johnson's proposal would avoid a roughly 22 percent benefit cut by covering the gap with borrowing. It is meant to keep Republicans from being pushed into a payroll tax increase. She disagrees with the tactic but credits him. The hosts then turn to the Pan American Health Organization declaring that the U.S. has lost measles elimination status. They play Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. blaming pandemic-era vaccination declines, with MMR coverage falling from about 97 percent to 92.3 percent.

The panel debates measles and Kennedy's role. Strassel blames the Biden administration's COVID vaccine push for eroding trust, but says Kennedy has helped undermine faith in safe childhood vaccines. Vaccination rates have fallen below the 95 percent needed for herd immunity. The CDC reports 5,838 confirmed cases in 2026, with 11 percent hospitalized, including 177 children under five, and six deaths, the most since the early 1990s. Sternberg says the vaccines' success has led people to forget how dangerous measles is. Kindergarten coverage fell from 95.2 percent in 2019-20 to 92.4 percent in 2025-26, with Iowa at 88.9, Utah at 87.2 and Florida also low. Strassel faults Republican-led states for loosening exemptions, and says states and Washington, plus public health officials admitting COVID mistakes, must rebuild trust.
